comments.text: I started on Amiga with a Tracker, moved to an Atari ST+Cubase and an Akai S900 - that was all I could afford at 17. Years later I twiddled with ReBirth, then came FruityLoops, now I am like everyone else on Ableton .... and like it as much as I hate it. I don't feel, I actually KNOW for a fact that what I do today is TECHNICALLY more advanced, but CREATIVELY a shamble. The limtations back then and finding workarounds because I couldn't afford equipment made the results way more artistic then anything I do today. When I went DAWless a few years back I regained a bit of my old crativity, because there were no more plugins and everything had to be done again "by hand". Now, no time and too lazy, I went back to DAW and plugins, only occasionally turning some knobs ..... to a point where I think to sell most of my gear, keeping only a few essentials like only ONE of my many 303 clones (probably keeping the BassBot), my Erica Synth DB-1, my Syntakt and my Digitakt, and an old Quasimidi Quasar for nostalgia. Virus C, Octatrack, all the Roland Boutique and Aira stuff and all the other gadgets can go to Ebay. So, NO, we definitely don't need more gear.
comments.author: @Vurt.451

comments.text: Hi! One of my favorite tracks as well! I started out  making music on a PC with Fasttracker II at that time and one of the biggest limitations was that there was no algoritmic reverb(or delay/chorus for that matter). So you were fully dependent on the samples you could find or make and how you manipulate them. So for me at that time having a Qudraverb would be the dream.  Moved on to other software during the years and now you can do basically everything in the box. I still prefer a combination of both modern software and hardware when creating music as there is something with the tactile feeling as well as the limitations you find hardware equipment. Anyways, thank you for your music walkthroughs! Always great. Ps. I got my Qudraverb in the end and have used it on some of my tracks to get that "lofi" 90s sound. Not sure if anyone actually can hear it 😏

comments.text:
i have a hardware rack. i believe, with some level of honesty, that i'm of a dying tribe.  in the rack: Quadraverb GT, a Samson TRS patchbay, an Alesis reference amplifier, and a TEAC A300.  
granted, i've a bunch of drum machines, modern external FX units (Reminder, SpecTemp, OBNE) on the shelf, and my most prized piece of gear, a CS1x rompler from 1998. is any of this high-fidelity? absolutely not. do i have fun goofing off and recording to tape? i do. 

please understand: this is NOT a statement of hardware superiority.  nothing made me happier than ReBirth 338 when it was released!  I have a modern DAW and a softsynth i just love- i simply prefer faders and knobs and physical gonking- and have nothing but respect and admiration for those creatives using software suites. more power to you and your creativity!

comments.text:
"Do You Need Hardware to Make Music Like Aphex Twin?" I love my hardware but nope. Personally I'd just use Bitwig. No extra plugins required. 

Now if I want it to sound like Aphex Twin, I would def consider what hardware he might have used, and where. If I don't have the hardware I'd test the software equivalents, if they exists. Failing that, I'd try to mimic the sound using the next closest software alternative. New hardware would be my last option, if I really wanted a specific sound that bad.
comments.author: @EnervatedSociety

comments.text:
I've been to an "electronic music production" workshop yesterday and while I turn 2 knobs to get my delay pedal SOUND right and activating my sidechain pedal takes one button, the tutor was fiddling for ten minutes with a million settings and half a dozen plugins, pulling things to "minus 6.02" and stuff to make it LOOK right. So to me, it's A LOT LESS knobs, not more.

Do you NEED hardware to make music? No. But my life is a lot essier and enjoyable without 5000 plugins. I make music by LISTENING to it, not by entering digits from an excel sheet 😖

comments.text:
The original QuadraVerb was designed by Marcus Ryle and Michel Doidic (who also designed the Oberheim DMX, OB-Xa, Xpander, Matrix-12, invented ADAT, and founded Line 6). I think the MidiVerb 2 (with the good reverse reberb all the shoegaze bands use) was also designed by them. Those are super legit. They have over 20 dBu headroom. The QV has a VCA on the dry side so you can even use it as a MIDI-controlled analog mixer. All the newer ones like the MidiVerb 4 and QuadraVerb 2 and later are completely different with cheap components.

I basically did the same thing and bought a MidiVerb 4 and it's pretty bad. But now I have two QuadraVerbs. The QV has such a good/simple interface. The front says QuadraVerb 20K Bandwidth because in 1989 most FX had a much lower cutoff because nothing had oversampling and you need everything to roll off before 22k. It's the ultimate retro reverb because it's old-school and can be huge but it's also got a completely analog dry path and a ton of headroom so it keeps the clean signal clean. It doesn't just run the input directly into an ADC.

Rack FX are some of the only things that are still cheap. You can still get an SPX90 for under $200, and QuadraVerbs pop up for that price pretty regularly... although they are well-known enough that a lot of people on Reverb list them for stupid prices and just leave them there. I mean I wouldn't use a QV for a 'normal' reverb. If you want a normal Valhalla-y hardware reverb I think the Eventide Blackhole/Space are the good ones. And I've seen used Space pedals for $200.

comments.text:
I had a quadraverb the same one aphex used and it was a very noisy unit..that's one of the reasons you'll not get the exact same sound using the version 2.
Version 1 added higher harmonic tones on the reverb which does sound nice and when you run audio through it it masks the constant noise..but once no audio is passed through it it was annoying.
I used it and had a noise gate too stop any unwanted noise coming from the unit.

Another really good fx unit from back in the day was the zoom 1201 fx unit...that was used on tons of rave records and had a pretty good vocoder on it too.
That too had a bit of noise but wasn't as bad.

Aphex and most people back then didn't use quadravebs by choice they used them because they were very cheap and that's all you could afford from turnkey 😂
Really miss turnkey and sound control ❤❤
